title: ACD routing
summary: Standard, bullseye, preferred, predictive, and conditional routing, plus the two scoring methods.

lessons.title: Five routing methods
lessons.summary: Standard, predictive, bullseye, preferred agent, and conditional group routing are the methods on a queue.
paras: The routing settings article lists those five. Standard is the default. It offers the interaction to the next agent according to the evaluation method you picked. Bullseye adds rings that widen the pool. Preferred agent tries a named pool first. Predictive uses historical outcomes against a KPI you select. Conditional group routing shares a group of agents across queues when a KPI rule says the other queue can spare them.

Methods can time out into another method. Preferred agent’s timeout can fall back to standard, bullseye, or conditional group routing. Predictive’s timeout falls back to standard. If you only memorize the names, you will mis-set the fallback and the queue will look “stuck” when it is doing the second method.

lessons.title: All skills, best available, or disregard
lessons.summary: The evaluation method is how standard and bullseye decide that an agent “has the skills.”
paras: All skills matching selects the longest-idle agent who has every required skill. Proficiency is not the sort. Best available skills looks at the 100 longest-idle agents who have the required skills and then picks the highest average proficiency, with idle time as the tie-break. Disregard skills, next agent, offers the interaction to the first available agent and ignores skills.

The evaluation article also says routing considers agent activity from the previous 7 days and skips inactive agents. A skill you added this morning on an agent who has not been active does not behave like a skill on someone who has been taking calls all week. Bullseye’s strict rings want all-skills or best-available. Disregard skills makes the rings much less meaningful.

figure.caption: All-skills sorts by idle time. Best-available sorts by proficiency inside the idle window.

lessons.title: Conversation score and priority score
lessons.summary: One priority point on conversation score is worth 60,000 milliseconds of arrival time.
paras: Conversation score combines arrival time and priority. The evaluation article says one priority point equals 60,000 milliseconds, so a higher priority jumps the line as if it had arrived earlier. Priority score uses the priority value first and time-in-queue only as a tie-break. When queues that the same agent serves use different scoring methods, Genesys Cloud gives precedence to queues using priority score.

A priority 5 interaction that arrived now outranks a priority 0 interaction that arrived four minutes ago, because five points are 300,000 milliseconds, which is five minutes. That arithmetic is the article’s rule, and it is the rule the routing simulator uses. It is not a reason to set every queue to priority 10. If everything is urgent, nothing is.

lessons.title: Bullseye rings widen the target
lessons.summary: Up to five rings. A delay from 2 seconds to 72 hours. Up to 50 skills removed on a ring.
paras: Bullseye starts with the tightest pool and expands. The settings article allows five rings. The delay between rings is from 2 seconds through 259,200 seconds, which is 72 hours. A ring can remove up to 50 skills. Two expansion styles are documented: add groups that share the skill at a lower proficiency, which stays compatible with WEM forecasting, or remove skills on outer rings.

Inner-ring agents stay preferred over outer-ring agents even after the ring opens. Preferred agents are considered even when they lack the required skills. Agents who are busy, fully utilized, or logged out are not available. The routing simulator in this lab removes a skill on ring 2 after the ring 1 delay, which is the skill-removal style, not a second product.

lessons.title: Preferred agents are tried first
lessons.summary: A preferred agent is considered even without the required skills, and only if they are a member of the queue and On Queue.
paras: The behavior article describes a score and a timeout. In its example the first window tries the highest-score preferred agent, and the next window opens the rest of the preferred pool. Selection among agents who meet the current score is by time since the last interaction. Full utilization removes an agent from consideration. Partial utilization does not. If no preferred agent is actually a member of the queue, the timeouts are skipped and routing moves on.

Last-agent routing does not apply to email flows, only to direct queue routing in the cases the article allows. During transfers, preferred agents are excluded. A higher-priority interaction still jumps ahead of a preferred match for a lower-priority one. The simulator’s “preferred first” switch is this idea: if any preferred agent is eligible, the pool is only those agents.

lessons.title: Predictive routing is a KPI model with a timeout
lessons.summary: Predictive routing can run for everyone, in a comparison test, or at a fixed 80/20 split you cannot edit.
paras: The queue article describes three modes. Comparison test mode measures predictive routing against a baseline. Use for all interactions sends everything through the model. Ongoing value monitoring keeps an 80 percent predictive and 20 percent baseline split, and the article says you cannot change that ratio. Genesys recommends leaving monitoring in place for months. The timeout still falls back to standard routing. If the queue has no interactions for 30 continuous days, predictive routing turns itself off and standard routing returns.

The model needs history. A queue you created this morning does not have a KPI story yet. Comparison mode is how you earn the right to turn it on for everyone. The AI certification catalog treats predictive routing and predictive engagement as a study path of their own. Turning the feature on is not the same as passing that exam, and it is not the same as bullseye.

lessons.title: Conditional group routing borrows agents carefully
lessons.summary: A rule is a KPI plus agent availability. The other queue must be able to spare the people.
paras: The overview describes conditional group routing as sharing groups of agents between queues based on rules. A rule combines a KPI with availability so you do not pull agents off a queue that is already missing its service level. The settings article says you can build up to five rules. It is a routing method, not a bullseye ring and not a WFM schedule change.

Use it when two queues are real neighbors, such as billing and billing overflow, and you can name the KPI that protects the donor queue. Do not use it as a silent way to empty a specialist queue. The agents still have to be On Queue, under utilization, and allowed by whatever evaluation method the target queue is using.

lessons.title: Utilization and Not Responding
lessons.summary: A fully utilized agent is skipped. An agent who ignores an alert becomes Not Responding.
paras: Defaults from the utilization article: one voice call, one email, one callback, up to four chats, up to four messages, and up to four workitems. You can change the org default and a single agent. You can also decide which medias may interrupt which others. By default, calls and callbacks do not interrupt each other. Non-ACD calls are excluded unless you enable “Count non-ACD calls in utilization capacity” and set voice capacity to 1, which stops ACD alerts during personal calls.

Voice alerting is 7 to 59 seconds. When it expires, the agent’s status becomes Not Responding and the interaction returns to the queue. Auto answer removes the alerting timeout, though the agent still gets an audio alert. Preview calls count as callbacks. The preferred-agent article uses the same utilization idea: a full agent is not offered the interaction.
